abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND We describe the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) Biomarker Core major activities from October 2004 to March 2024, including biobanking ADNI cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), plasma, and serum biofluid samples, biofluid analyses for Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers in the Biomarker Core and various non‐ADNI laboratories, and continuous assessments of pre‐analytics. RESULTS Validated immunoassay and mass spectrometry‐based assays were performed in CSF with a shift to plasma, a more accessible biofluid, as qualified assays became available. Performance comparisons across different CSF and plasma AD biomarker measurement platforms have enriched substantially the ADNI participant database enabling method performance determinations for AD pathology detection and longitudinal assessments of disease progression. DISCUSSION Close collaboration with academic and industrial partners in the validation and implementation of AD biomarkers for early detection of disease pathology in treatment trials and ultimately in clinical practice is a key factor for the success of the work done in the Biomarker Core. Highlights Describe ADNI Biomarker Core biobanking and sample distribution from 2007 to 2024. Discuss validated mass spectrometry and immunoassay methods for ADNI biofluid analyses. Review collaborations with academic and industrial partners to detect AD and progression. Discuss major challenges, and progress to date, for co‐pathology detection. Implementation in the ATN scheme: co‐pathology and modeling disease progression.

body:
1
BACKGROUND
In this review, we first summarize the major activities in two aspects of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) Biomarker Core, namely, (1) all functions associated with biofluid specimen receipt, processing, maintenance of biofluids, shipment on dry ice by ADNI clinical sites, and storage in dedicated ‐80°C freezers in the ADNI Biobank at the University of Pennsylvania (UPENN), and (2) the distribution of these specimens to investigators who make requests via the Resource Allocation Review Committee (RARC). Second, we discuss biofluid biomarker pre‐analytics and measurements performed by the ADNI Biomarker Core in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and more recently in plasma including validation and cut‐point determinations for individual or combinations of proteins. Third, we review the ongoing collaborations of the Biomarker Core with investigators from around the globe, including studies designed to assess the diagnostic performance of CSF and plasma Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers for the detection of AD pathology and the prediction of cognitive decline. Finally, we consider the newest developments in the field of AD biofluid biomarkers to determine which new biomarkers the Biomarker Core will seek to include in future ADNI Phases and the associated pre‐analytics and validation studies needed.
During the first year of the ADNI4 phase, John Q. Trojanowski sadly passed away. We dedicate this review to John as a tribute to his enormous contributions to the field of AD and other neurological diseases of biomarker research in all of its dimensions, including fundamental studies he and his life partner Virginia M.‐Y. Lee continually produced and consistently strong support for the development of biofluid biomarkers from defining them through to regulatory approvals for their use in the clinic. John's memory and track record inspire many in the AD field to continue their work, especially now validating and implementing blood‐based biomarkers in clinical trials and, ultimately, in clinical practice.
An essential aspect of the development and continued work has been close collaboration with academic and industrial partners who are dedicated to the validation and implementation of AD biomarkers for early detection of disease pathology in treatment trials and clinical practice.
1
,
2
Over the years the work of the ADNI Biomarker Core has benefitted from close working relationships with both academic and industrial scientists–colleagues. This review will reflect on all these joint efforts that made it possible to perform clinical studies and publication of the work done.
NOTE
: Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the ADNI database (adni.loni.usc.edu). The ADNI was launched in 2003 as a public–private partnership, led by principal investigator Michael W. Weiner, MD. The primary goal of ADNI has been to test whether serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early Alzheimer's disease (AD).
2
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
2.1
Biofluid Biobank at UPENN
From the beginning of the ADNI1 study to the present day, the Biomarker Core has continuously received biofluid samples (CSF, EDTA‐plasma, serum; urine in ADNI1 only) shipped from all ADNI sites {(Laboratory of Neuro Imaging (LONI) website, for details of ADNI biofluid standard operating procedures [SOPs] for sample processing:
https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data‐samples/access‐data/
)}, followed by aliquoting, labeling and monitoring 24 h/7 day (24/7) in dedicated ‐80°C freezers at UPENN. Back‐up freezers are available whenever needed. Biomarker Core staff continue to work closely with Clinical Core staff and clinical sites performing daily reconciliation of essential details for each collected sample. For each phase, the ADNI SOPs include the detailed preanalytical procedures in use for sample preparation at ADNI sites. We follow best practices for sample processing. In contrast to other studies or consortia, the total volume of collected fluid is shipped on dry ice via overnight shipping, followed by aliquot preparation and labeling and storage in ‐80°C freezers with 24/7 temperature monitoring.
3
,
4
As summarized in Figure
1
a total of 3267 CSF, 11,378 plasma, and 11,360 serum samples were collected from 1677 to 2737 unique individuals for CSF and plasma/serum, respectively, collected from August 2005 to February 2024. Biomarker Core staff provide biofluid samples to investigators who propose to study new candidate biomarkers or novel improved methods for core biomarkers, after approval by the National Institute on Aging (NIA)/ADNI/Resource Allocation Review Committee (RARC) and ADNI leadership (see ADNI website for a description of the RARC and a summary of biofluids shipped to approved investigators‐from December 2007 to March 2024—see Table “Summary of ADNI CSF, Plasma, Serum and Whole Blood aliquots distributed to RARC‐approved Investigators” on the ADNI LONI website, [
https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data‐samples/access‐data/
] and overall summary in Figure
1
. During the time from December 2007 to March 2024, a total of 38,405 sample aliquots (25,443 plasma, 9815 CSF, and 3147 serum) were distributed to investigators. Given the richness of the phenotypic data, collected longitudinally on each ADNI participant, and which is freely available from the ADNI repository, the ADNI study has in turn benefitted from the contributions of investigators who obtain approval for their study from the NIA/ADNI/RARC. In subsequent sections, we highlight some of these studies and acknowledge all of them in the Table available online: “Summary of ADNI CSF, Plasma, Serum and Whole Blood aliquots distributed to RARC‐approved investigators.”
RESEARCH IN CONTEXT
Systematic review
: Literature was reviewed using traditional sources such as PubMed as well as our internal records within the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative ADNI) Biomarker Core at University of Pennsylvania (UPENN), ADNI, and other meetings and presentations and in consultation with academic and industrial colleague‐experts in the biofluid biomarker field.
Interpretation
: We describe the progress made in transitioning from the “legacy” research use only (RUO) to in vitro diagnostic‐level highly automated immunoassays for Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers in all cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collected from participants since ADNI began through the ADNI3 phase. Based upon many lessons learned regarding identifying and controlling pre‐analytical variables, and design and implementation of validation studies of CSF AD biomarker tests, and extensive consultation with academic and industrial biomarker scientists, the ADNI Biomarker Core has implemented the most promising plasma biomarker tests: Aβ42/Aβ40 and p‐tau217 using highly automated immunoassays and other informative biomarkers, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) using high‐sensitivity immunoassays and with collaboration of the C2N team, mass‐spectrometry based tests for Aβ42/Aβ40 and p‐tau217/np‐tau217 in the “remote blood” and “in‐clinic” ADNI4 participants.
Future directions
: Plasma AD biomarker testing in more diverse populations is needed to assess the performance of these new tests in settings more real‐world. Continued progress in reliable detection of co‐pathologies including α‐SYN for Lewy Body co‐pathology and detection and quantification of TDP‐43.

CSF Aβ42, p‐tau181, and total tau (t‐tau) measured using the INNO‐BIA AlzBio3 micro‐bead‐based research‐use‐only (RUO) xMAP immunoassay during the ADNI1, ADNIGO and ADNI2 phases
From the inception of the ADNI1 study, and throughout the ADNIGO and ADNI2 phases of the study, all CSF β‐amyloid 1‐42 (Aβ42), t‐tau, and phosphorylated tau 181 (p‐tau181) concentration measurements were made using the micro‐bead‐based multiplex immunoassay, “xMAP,” the INNO‐BIA AlzBio3 RUO test (Fujirebio [formerly Innogenetics], Ghent, Belgium),

developed on the xMAP technology (Luminex) platform. The xMAP Luminex system is a flow cytometric‐based platform that can simultaneously detect several analytes on different sets of microspheres in a single well.
5

Included in this micro‐bead based immunoassay system were color‐coded carboxylated polystyrene beads, covalently coupled with capture monoclonal antibodies, covalently linked to the polystyrene microbeads, specific for Aβ42 (4D7A3)
,
t‐tau (AT120, epitope, amino acids (a.a) 218‐224]), and p‐tau181 (AT270, epitope 176‐182]). Included in the reagent mixture were a combination of two biotinylated detector monoclonal antibodies which can detect all together the three analytes for each analyte (3D6, specific for Aβ42; epitope: a.a. 1‐5) + (HT7, specific for detection of t‐tau and p‐tau181; epitope: a.a. 159‐163).
5

7
Before implementing this platform and reagents into the Biomarker Core, we conducted extensive within‐ and between‐laboratory validation studies using non‐ADNI CSF samples.

2
A more complete description of the detailed planning and execution of this study and results can be found in the publication.

aliquots were reported on the ADNI website and subsequently described in the peer‐reviewed literature.

42

181

Precision performance within the Biomarker Core throughout these studies was < 10%, and clinical performance met our expectations. At the time ADNI1 was initiated (2004), there was general agreement that: “The ideal biomarker for AD should detect a fundamental feature of neuropathology and be validated in neuropathologically‐confirmed cases; it should have a diagnostic sensitivity > 80% for detecting AD and a specificity of > 80% for distinguishing other dementias; it should be reliable, reproducible, noninvasive, simple to perform, and inexpensive.”

11
A head‐to‐head study comparing performance to that of the then widely used enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methodology demonstrated equivalence of these two RUO immunoassays versus amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) (Pittsburgh Compound B;PiB).
12
Although this analytical platform performed well in our Biomarker Core laboratory there were at that point in time several shortcomings including a highly complex set of manual steps; lack of a certified reference material for calibrator standardization for each analyte; difficulties in achieving inter‐laboratory performance of < 10% CV; considerable lot‐to‐lot variability necessitating inclusion of “bridging” replicate CSF samples with each new batch of reagents; and poor performance across multiple laboratories with interlaboratory %CV values reported as high as > 20% for CSF Aβ42.
13
Although technically feasible, no second generation of the assay format was commercialized by the vendor. Thus, although we were able to provide very good CSF Aβ42, t‐tau and p‐tau181 data for the ADNI study as well as in a number of collaborative investigations,
14
we sought an improved platform for analyses of ADNI samples in the ADNI3 phase. A summary report for the eight analytical batch runs using the AlzBio3 xMAP‐based platform performed from 2008 to 2015 can be found on the Laboratory of Neuroimaging (LONI) ADNI website: [see Methods document, “UPENN CSF Biomarker Master AlzBio3 Methods (Batch 1‐8) [ADNI1, GO, 2]” (
https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data‐samples/access‐data/
). The limitations of the AlzBio3 immunoassay led the Biomarker Core to seek an improved analytical platform and reagents. The automation of sample handling for the xMAP platform in the Biomarker Core

2.3
Transition to a fully automated analytical platform and accompanying reagents, the Roche Elecsys Cobas e601 platform and reagents
During the latter part of ADNI2, the Biomarker Core together with ADNI leadership, consulted with leaders in the AD biofluid biomarkers field and worked with the ADNI Private Partners Scientific Board (PPSB) Biofluid Biomarkers Working Group [see Section
2.6.2
for additional details]. Following systematic reviews and discussions of the commercially available immunoassays, together with the documented performance data available at that time, the decision was made to validate and then implement the Roche Elecsys fully automated immunoassay platform and reagents. The latter were used for analysis of CSF Aβ42, t‐tau, and p‐tau181 in all available ADNI1/GO/2 CSF samples.

A research level immunoassay for Aβ40 was included in the analyses, using the Elecsys platform, of the ADNI3 CSFs which permitted inclusion of the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio in this dataset. Several studies provided evidence for the added value of using the Aß42/Aß40 ratio instead of Aß42 alone, not only for standardization at the analytical level by removal of adsorption problems of Aß42 to tubes, but also to obtain improved clinical performance.

2.4
Studies to establish reference methodology and Certified Reference Materials (CRMs) for CSF Aβ42 and Aβ40
At the time of the first ADNI phase, the two most widely used immunoassay methods in the field, ELISA INNOTEST and the xMAP INNO‐BIA AlzBio3 (both from Innogenetics[Fujirebio]), had a difference in mean measured concentrations of Aβ42 in a common set of CSF samples of about three‐fold! That fact and the observed significant center‐to‐center variability largely precluded global standardization and the ability to establish uniform cutoff values for these RUO immunoassays. This was considered a major impediment to using these assays.

2.5
Moving from CSF to blood‐based biomarkers for reliable detection of AD pathology in clinical trials and clinical practice
Although Aβ PET and CSF AD biomarkers are well established as validated surrogates for detection of AD pathology,

,

2.5.1
Plasma sample pre‐analytics
Regarding pre‐analytic aspects, it became clear to us during the ADNI3 Phase in the ADNI Biomarker Core, that a critical review of blood processing before freezing, was important and critical given our expectation that much more need for ADNI plasma samples was a great likelihood. Thus, we undertook a detailed review of our plasma sample preparation protocol and actual performance across all ADNI sites. We reviewed the timing for all steps in the preparation of plasma and changed one step in the process, namely, the time from collection to centrifugation. A pharma biomarker evaluation study done by Innogenetics in collaboration with Eli Lilly revealed decreased plasma Aβ42 concentrations even after storage for a few hours at 2–8°C
58
and the fact that measurement of Aβ proteoforms would be very difficult or even impossible with the technologies available at that time. The study also showed better detection of Aβ proteoforms in EDTA‐plasma as compared to serum samples. The modified protocol, implemented in ADNI in 2019 reduced the median time blood samples stood at room temperature to 30 min or less by starting plasma preparation immediately after blood draw and proper blood sample mixing in the EDTA tube, instead of waiting a ½ h as required for serum sample preparation to assure completion of blood sample clotting. We have documented completion of plasma sample total preparation time to within 1 h across all ADNI sites, including the six sites with prolonged specimen processing time that we discovered during this review. We express continued appreciation to all ADNI sites for their attention to these important details that assure best possible sample quality in support of AD biomarker studies. The ADNI study continues to collect timing information for each step in the sample preparation process as invaluable sample specific history information. Based on the detailed studies of pre‐analytical factors’ influence on plasma samples
4
,
57
the 1 h plasma preparation time at ADNI sites before shipment on dry ice provides for an effective sample preparation time that is expected to control the very important pre‐analytical sample preparation process.
2.5.2
A cautionary note regarding the potential impact of confounding factors on plasma biomarker concentration values
Several studies have concluded that certain confounding factors such as abnormal body mass index (BMI) or chronic kidney disease or race, can affect the concentration values obtained and therefore might alter the accuracy of assessment of presence or absence of AD pathology based on plasma biomarker results.
86
,
87
At this time, we believe it is important to continue vigilance and studies of these and any other potential confounding factors. We are fully engaged in the ADNI4 study in measuring plasma biomarkers in the planned enriched representation by the URPs study, included in the ADNI4 study plan.
84
,
85
The recruitment process in the ADNI4 study includes a larger percentage of URPs than possible in earlier ADNI Phases, is more representative of the US elderly population, and is actively underway.
85
This study which includes digital screening for cognitive status, as well as performance of plasma AD biomarker tests (summarized in Table
2
), will hopefully provide for substantial documentation on effects, if any, of race or socioeconomic status, on the accuracy of AD pathology diagnosis. We are engaged in studies in non‐ADNI populations including a UPENN ADRC cohort
88
plus a further ADRC cohort, and a PENN MEDICINE Biobank population that will provide a substantial increased number of URPs that should provide additional data on this issue. We agree with the conclusion that factors such as BMI and chronic kidney disease can potentially have an impact on the clinical accuracy when using plasma biomarkers for AD detection, but maybe it is not an issue for the majority of individuals.
86
We appreciate that this rapidly progressing field will require additional studies in populations beyond the most frequently studied ones‐symptomatic groups with suspected AD pathology. The clinical utility of these tests in the broader population, for example, in primary care or for screening healthy individuals, where the prevalence of AD is substantially lower, will need to be assessed.
89
2.5.3
Selection of analytical platforms and biomarkers for use in ADNI4
During the second half of ADNI3, Biomarker Core leadership and staff together with ADNI leadership engaged in frequent discussions regarding selection of analytical platforms, specific biomarkers that would be measured, and the labs in which they would be performed. A part of that process was continuous consultation with the Public Private Scientific Board (PPSB) Biofluid Biomarker Working Group (BBWG). ADNI leadership together with the BBWG invited all known, at the time, developers of plasma biomarker tests to provide detailed summaries of study data, supporting the development and application of their tests in various populations. These presentations and the results of the Foundation of the National Institutes of Health Biomarker Consortium (FNIH BC) and ADNI “Comparative analytical performance of multiple plasma Aβ42 and Aβ40 assays and their ability to predict positron emission tomography amyloid positivity” study
53
were extremely helpful in providing a data‐driven basis for method selection for plasma AD biomarker tests in the ADNI4 study. Several assay manufacturers indicated their intent to obtain regulatory approval as in vitro diagnostic devices, which in the United States includes several companies with Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Breakthrough Device program status.
2.6
Collaboration with industrial biomarker scientists
The ADNI PPSB is a distinctive component of the ADNI. Commissioned to provide collaborative oversight and dialogue, PPSB serves as an independent advisory board, bringing together representatives from the private sector, including pharmaceutical companies, biotechnology firms, diagnostic companies, and contract research organizations. It also includes members from nonprofit organizations that have provided financial and scientific support.
90
For the first three phases of ADNI, this occurred through the FNIH, whereas for the ADNI4 Phase the NIA is providing 100% of funding while the Alzheimer's Association convenes the ADNI PPSB meetings and functions. Unlike traditional scientific boards, the precompetitive nature of the PPSB fosters open dialogue, allowing diverse stakeholders to actively engage and provide strategic guidance. The openness of the PPSB reflects the general philosophy of ADNI with regards to open science, as ADNI represents the first major study to release qualified data in real time for the entire scientific community to use. The insights of the PPSB help ensure that ADNI remains aligned with cutting‐edge approaches and best practices. The relationships between the PPSB member organizations and the ADNI academic cores have progressively increased over time, including the commission of working groups to address questions outside the scope of the ADNI/ADNI Academic Cores.
2.6.1
First contribution of PPSB
The first contribution of the PPSB, regarding fluid biomarkers, was in 2010 as funding via the FNIH‐BC to complete multiplex proteomic analyses for plasma and CSF by Myriad/Rules Based Medicine, followed by similar multiplex and targeted CSF analyses, as well as more widespread CSF profiling.
91
Data from these studies were included in the ADNI repository, and several discovery projects (against clinical and pathology reference standards) were undertaken, with validation in external cohorts.

,

,

2.6.2
Established
Through collaboration with the ADNI Biomarker Core, the PPSB initiated a BBWG in 2012 to actively support and accelerate biomarker discovery and validation across both CSF and blood‐based biomarkers. This working group continues to be highly active today, in 2024. The BBWG facilitated closer interaction with diagnostic companies to address gaps for biofluid assay validation and clinical
93
qualification. The increasing use of CSF for AD biomarkers as a trial enrichment strategy and the potential for a companion diagnostic, with associated regulatory and technical requirements, was a key driver of this. Samples from ADNI2 and ADNI‐GO for clinical validation against amyloid‐PET as the reference standard were used to support the successful FDA 510(k) and CE mark submissions for Roche Elecsys immunoassays (see discussion in Section 3).
19
,
21
,
95
Additionally, after due diligence to evaluate different CSF assays, the BBWG recommended Roche Elecsys evaluations be included in ADNI3, moving from a pre‐ to post‐competitive space. This led the BBWG in partnership with the Core to develop a transparent and fair process for access to previously thawed (not fresh aliquots) CSF samples to appropriately support vendors/companies developing commercial IVD tests. All resultant data has been included in the ADNI repository. To date, Fujirebio, Euroimmun, Meso Scale Diagnostics, and Saladex have accessed samples through this process. The successful FDA and CE mark submissions by Fujirebio were strongly supported by the inclusion of the ADNI CSF samples together with the corresponding amyloid PET reference standard data.

,

2.6.3
PPSB BBWG focuses on blood‐based AD biomarkers
Recently, there has been a rapid increase in the development of blood‐based biomarkers that identify AD pathology with an accuracy comparable to CSF biomarkers. Given their lower cost and increased accessibility, blood‐based biomarkers have the potential to revolutionize and democratize clinical diagnosis and management. Efforts have been split across assay development and validation, with clinical validation against reference standards including neuropathology, PET, and CSF, as well as longitudinal change and natural history evaluation being key foci for the BBWG. Numerous assays have been evaluated in ADNI samples by academic groups as well as Roche, Fujirebio, ADx Neurosciences (now part of the Fujirebio group), Shimadzu, ADx, Quanterix, and C2N as described in Section 2.7.2 on the Biomarker Consortium of the FNIH.
2.6.4
PPSB BBWG beyond ADNI4
As ADNI continues (including ADNI4 and beyond), the PPSB's activities will address gaps and further refinements in biomarker research, ensuring that fluid biomarkers continue to gain traction as valuable tools in the fight against AD. The PPSB BBWG's collaborative approach, global impact, and strategic guidance make it a unique and essential component of ADNI's groundbreaking efforts in AD biomarker research, which continues to benefit patients, researchers, industry, and the broader scientific community.
2.7
Working with the Foundation of the NIH Biomarker Consortium (FNIH‐BC)
2.7.1
First proteomic plasma and CSF studies in ADNI
The first project developed and funded by the FNIH‐BC for investigation of candidate new analytes beyond the established amyloid and tau‐based biomarkers in CSF or plasma was devoted to exploratory studies using a multiplex, xMAP Luminex immunoassay platform for CSF and plasma
94
,
98
,
99
noted in 2.6.1 above. This immunoassay‐based study was followed by a targeted LC/MSMS based proteomic investigation “Use of Targeted Mass Spectrometry Proteomic Strategies to Identify CSF‐Based Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease”
91
that included detection of 142 proteins based upon 320 peptides derived from them by a proteolytic digestion step. This latter study that included 285 baseline CSF samples (85 cognitively normal controls, 134 MCI, 66 AD) from ADNI participants was followed by an FNIH‐BC sponsored investigation of the five most promising new candidates (aside from other known promising new biomarkers (NfL, neurogranin, VILIP‐1, and YKL‐40): Chromogranin A, fatty acid binding protein, neuronal pentraxin 2 (NPTX2), secretogranin and neurosecretory protein VGF.

The other feature of this investigation was inclusion of at least three longitudinal samples from each participant to permit interrogation of longitudinal changes in these biomarkers in relationship to disease presence based on CSF AD biomarkers and disease progression clinically. Of these five candidate biomarkers, CSF concentration of NPTX2, a marker of synaptic function,

,
102

Furthermore, NPTX2 concentration was significantly lower in AD pathology positive versus negative (defined by CSF ptau181/Aβ42 ratio) individuals and in clinical progressors versus nonprogressors.
100
This and other studies support the utility of NPTX2 as a marker of synaptic plasticity with changes occurring as early as amyloid plaque burden does in the AD continuum.

In an investigator‐initiated study, a targeted MRM LC/MSMS analysis of a panel of 48 biomarkers, selected based on earlier work, was completed in 706 ADNI participant (220 cognitively normal/376 MCI/110 AD dementia) CSF samples.

This study found that both FDG PET and hippocampal volume were positively associated with decreased concentrations of NPTX2 and its receptor protein NPTX2R (correlation coefficient

Comparison of performance of recently developed assays of Aβ42/Aβ40 and longitudinal assessment of ptau and other AD biomarkers
In response to the development of improved assays for Aβ42/Aβ40 in plasma,

The initial study included three immunoassays (Roche Elecsys, Quanterix 4‐plex N4PE, and duplex tests) and three mass spectrometry assays (2 IP‐LC/MSMS and 1 MALDI TOF).

Assays from C2N Diagnostics‐PrecivityAD2 (an algorithm based on a combination of Aβ42/Aβ40 and the p‐tau217/non‐p‐tau217 ratios), Roche Diagnostics Elecsys platform (Aβ42/Aβ40, p‐tau181, GFAP, NfL), Fujirebio‐Lumipulse platform (Aβ42/Aβ40, p‐tau217), AlzPath‐Simoa platform (p‐tau217), Janssen‐Simoa platform (p‐tau217), and Quanterix‐Simoa platform (Aβ42/Aβ40, p‐tau181, GFAP, NfL) were performed on three longitudinal plasma samples from 392 ADNI participants (1176 samples total). 2.8
Future directions
In this review, we have highlighted the work of the ADNI Biomarker Core on standardization of AD biomarker measurements in biofluids to support their use in drug development and ultimately in clinical practice and support of the study of new biomarker tests collaborating, for example, in the application of multiplex proteomic methods with our pharmaceutical and academic colleagues. As we consider future needs in the field we predict there will be increased attention paid to the development of tests to detect mixed pathology. The first study we have been involved with is the inclusion of a semiquantitative test, α‐synuclein seeding amplification assay, for α‐synuclein, and we expect further developments of this testing in the future and requisite validation studies. We anticipate further development of test methods for TDP‐43 another major example of a mixed pathology. In the following discussion, we describe the basis for future consideration of these and other biomarker tests we hope will add to the existing value of tests for amyloid plaque and tau tangle burden for detection of AD pathology and predicting in a more fine‐grained manner, cognitive decline in affected individuals.
2.8.1
Mixed pathology in AD
While AD is defined by the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles,
108
post mortem
autopsy studies have demonstrated that dementia is associated with remarkable diversity in terms of the prevalence and severity of other comorbid neurodegenerative disease pathologic changes. Indeed, a major feature of AD is the common occurrence of co‐pathology detectable upon neuropathologic examination,
109
such as concomitant Lewy body disease (LBD), transactive response DNA binding protein of 43 kDa (TDP‐43) pathology, and neurovascular pathology. The remarkable heterogeneity of neuropathologies observed at autopsy is currently a challenge for a biomarker‐based diagnosis for two reasons: (1) pathological heterogeneity may alter AD biofluid levels and interpretation, and (2) a precise in vivo diagnosis requires accurate biomarker testing for and detection of multiple comorbidities beyond AD. The importance of understanding the interacting mechanisms of multiple pathologies is fundamental in the era of amyloid immunotherapies, where treatment efficacy may be affected when multiple pathologies are present; thus, future AD biomarker diagnostic strategies will require integration of testing for co‐pathologies. While significant progress in developing biomarkers for the
ante mortem
detection of amyloid and tau pathologies has been achieved, robust biomarkers for other types of neurodegenerative disease inclusions are just being developed.
Applying and interpreting AD biofluid biomarkers in non‐AD proteinopathies
Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are not only associated with AD amnestic dementia but are frequently concomitant in other proteinopathies including LBD.
110
LBD α‐synucleinopathies, which includes Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies, are primarily movement disorders, but cognitive symptoms in LBD have been linked to concomitant AD.
111
Indeed, substantial evidence shows that LBD individuals with AD‐positive CSF biomarkers show worse outcomes (e.g., cognition, language impairment, and postural instability/gait) than LBD with negative AD biomarkers.
112
,
113
,
114
Yet, even as AD biomarkers improve prognostic estimates in LBD, autopsy studies reveal that AD plasma and CSF biomarkers may be less sensitive to secondary AD pathology.
115
,
116
Thus, LBD‐specific biomarker strategies and cutoffs have been proposed that maximize the detection of concomitant AD in LBD.
117
,
118
The importance of testing AD biomarkers in non‐AD proteinopathies is further underlined by a surprising finding in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). While ALS is typically associated with TDP‐43 pathology and an absence of tau pathology, plasma p‐tau181 was elevated in our UPENN ALS cohort in association with lower motor neuron disease,
116
in addition to AD. This finding has since been replicated in independent ALS cohorts
119
,
120
providing important insight that plasma p‐tau may not be AD specific. Together these data show that it is not enough to test AD biomarker performance in AD amnestic dementia, but that heterogeneous pathologies can alter biomarker levels and interpretations. Moreover, patient factors like race, sex, and phenotype can influence biomarker levels and interpretation,
118
,
121
,
122
,
123
and more work is needed to investigate how these differences overlap with underlying pathological heterogeneity. Biomarkers therefore need to be validated in diverse cohorts that are representative of the demographic and pathological heterogeneity present in neurodegenerative diseases as discussed above in Section 5.2.
Mixed pathology in AD underscores the need for biomarkers of non‐AD pathology
There is consensus based on various autopsy cohort studies that “pure” AD, consisting of only amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, is relatively uncommon. The prevalence of comorbid neurodegenerative disease proteinopathies across cases within the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research (CNDR) brain bank at UPENN has been reported.
110
In cases with a high level of AD neuropathologic change, only 35% of autopsied cases exhibited only amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, with the other 65% of cases containing LBD and/or TDP‐43 proteinopathy (most commonly in the form of limbic‐predominant age‐related TDP‐43 encephalopathy, or LATE). The finding of comorbid proteinopathy in neurodegenerative disease cases was not limited to AD but rather was commonplace across a wide range of conditions including frontotemporal lobar degeneration and LBD. For example, only 19% of cases diagnosed with neocortical LBD exhibited a pure α‐synucleinopathy (αSyn) without beta‐amyloid, tau, or TDP‐43 aggregates. Notably, this analysis did not include assessment of cerebrovascular disease which would dramatically reduce the prevalence of pure AD even further.
Autopsy studies of the ADNI cohort revealed highly concordant results [see ref.
124
and Methods report posted on LONI [see Neuropathology Core review in this issue of Alzheimers and Dementia] and: ADNI_Neuropathology_Core_Methods_FINAL_20221114.pdf}]. From 2005 to 2024, 110 autopsies were performed among 216 reported deaths (autopsy rate of 51%). An important finding is that the accuracy of
ante mortem
clinical diagnosis of AD was very high at 92%. However, 69% of cases diagnosed clinically with AD (with or without dementia with Lewy bodies) exhibited other non‐AD comorbid neuropathologic changes. Interestingly, the high prevalence of comorbid neuropathologic change is also observed in autosomal dominant forms of AD, as evidenced by the presence of LBD pathology in 50% of autopsies from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network.
125
Another way to examine the heterogeneity within AD is to analyze the different types of combinations of neuropathology observed in each brain.
126
When considering clinical diagnoses, the CNDR brain bank includes cases that were categorized as unimpaired, AD, mixed etiology, motor neuron disease, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), tauopathy, LBD, and multiple system atrophy. A total of 10 different neuropathologic features that were present at moderate to severe levels were documented for each case. For example, a pure AD case would have a combination consisting of three neuropathologic findings corresponding to moderate to high Thal amyloid phase (A), Braak stage (B), and CERAD score (C). Remarkably, there were 161 unique neuropathology combinations for the 1647 cases examined. Moreover, the amount of heterogeneity in cases clinically diagnosed with AD was extensive, with 224 out of 453 AD cases exhibiting five to seven different neuropathologies.
Selection and referral bias is a common concern when it comes to interpreting results from tertiary, referral‐type medical center cohorts. However, data from community‐based autopsy cohorts are largely similar. The Religious Orders Study and the Rush Memory and Aging Project from Rush University boast a high annual follow‐up rate of over 90% with an autopsy rate that has historically neared 90%. In cases clinically diagnosed as probable AD, only 4 out of 447 cases (0.89%) exhibited only AD neuropathologic change when considering the breadth of neuropathologic change including the full spectrum of cerebrovascular disease (macroinfarcts, microinfarcts, moderate to severe atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, or cerebral amyloid angiopathy).
127
Importantly, each additional neuropathology increases the risk for AD dementia including cerebrovascular disease,
128
alpha‐synucleinopathy,
129
hippocampal sclerosis,
130
and other combinations.
131
Indeed, this autopsy cohort exhibited a remarkable 236 different neuropathology combinations among 1079 cases.
131
TDP‐43 and α‐synuclein pathologies are not only common in AD, but they are associated with worse cognitive outcomes.
132
Thus, an ongoing challenge is the development of biofluid biomarker tests that specifically detect non‐AD pathologies, and that can be integrated with the ATN framework to provide accurate detection of co‐pathologies and refine the prediction of decline. In particular, biomarkers for αSyn and TDP‐43 proteinopathy are now being developed and explored providing hope for a more comprehensive
ante mortem
biomarker armamentarium.
2.8.2
Emerging biomarker for αSyn
Concomitant αSyn‐containing Lewy body pathology is associated with a faster rate of progression, earlier onset of disease, and signs of parkinsonism including resting tremor, rigidity, and higher scores on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor score.
133
,
134
,
135
,
136
,
137
Yet, the role of concomitant αSyn in the progression of AD has not been well studied since, until recently, αSyn was only detectable via autopsy. A recent promising biomarker test for LBD is seed amplification assay (SAA)—the test for misfolded α‐synuclein in CSF that has high sensitivity and specificity for the detection of misfolded αSyn in persons with PD. The αSyn seed amplification assay (αSyn‐SAA) is adapted from diagnostic testing for prion diseases, whereby αSyn misfolding is induced via serial shaking or sonication in the presence of a pathogenic αSyn “seed” measured with a fluorescent tag.
138
CSF αSyn‐SAA has high sensitivity and specificity for PD and dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy and now serves as a biochemical test for PD.
139
Very promising results for detection of this major co‐pathology in AD have recently been reported in 119 pathology cases with various clinical syndromes demonstrating that
ante mortem
CSF αSyn‐SAA detects αSyn pathology in pathologically confirmed AD cases with high sensitivity and specificity, particularly in cases with neocortical Lewy bodies.
140
A study was recently conducted in CSF samples from ADNI participants including 577 CU, 654 MCI, and 407 dementia. This study included 77 participants who had an autopsy diagnosis.
141
The full details are described in a manuscript in this issue of Alzheimer's and Dementia.
141
Key findings are (1) an SAA positivity rate for αSyn pathology in the overall group of 22% with the largest frequency of positive results in the dementia group (37% dementia, 19% MCI, 16% CU); and (2) in the autopsy group SAA results had a sensitivity and specificity for detection of LB inclusions of 81% and 97%, respectively. The assay was significantly better in detecting neocortical compared to limbic and amygdala‐predominant LB pathology, confirming the results previously reported in an earlier study.
140
A noteworthy association was observed between increased prevalence of SAA+ and greater Aβ pathology burden but on the other hand lower tau pathology burden with increased SAA+ prevalence. Participants who were AD and SAA+ had poorer performance on a broad array of cognitive tests reflecting a wide spectrum of affected cognitive domains. The finding of lowered tau burden associated with SAA+ prevalence has been reported previously in PD.
112
2.8.3
Emerging biomarkers for TDP‐43 proteinopathy
TDP‐43 protein is a 43 kDa nuclear RNA‐binding protein with two RNA recognition motif domains and a C‐terminal glycine‐rich domain.
142
TDP‐43 inclusions are found in degenerating neurons in nearly all ALS cases (except rare variants associated with FUS or SOD1 mutations.
142
,
143
Aggregates of TDP‐43 are the primary pathology in the majority of FTD cases. Pathologic TDP‐43 exhibits multiple post‐translational modifications, including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and abnormal cleavage which generates C‐terminal fragments.
143
While TDP‐43 is normally localized to nuclei, neurons with cytoplasmic TDP‐43 inclusions exhibit a characteristic loss of normal nuclear TDP‐43 protein. Both the accumulation of cytoplasmic TDP‐43 aggregates and the loss of normal nuclear TDP‐43 have been postulated to coordinately result in neurotoxicity. Given that TDP‐43 protein forms aggregates in various neurodegenerative diseases, attempts to measure TDP‐43 from biofluids have yielded mixed results, although recent studies have suggested that extracellular vesicles from plasma of sporadic ALS may be somewhat elevated.
144
Similarly, using fluorescence‐activated cell sorting, astrocyte‐derived extracellular vesicles exhibited higher TDP‐43 protein levels by ELISA in LATE‐NC cases.
145
Finally, seeded amplification‐type reactions have been reported to detect TDP‐43 seeds in biological fluids from ALS and FTD cases.
146
Replication of these interesting findings will help determine whether exosomal TDP‐43 protein and/or TDP‐43 seeding activity can be used as a biomarker for TDP‐43 proteinopathy.
TDP‐43 regulates RNA on multiple levels, affecting pre‐mRNA splicing, miRNA biogenesis, mRNA stability, and mRNA transport. Consistent with its central role in regulating RNA metabolism, TDP‐43 binds to a large proportion of the entire transcriptome (> 39,000 transcript binding sites) and acute knockdown of TDP‐43 in mice expression leads to widespread changes in splicing and transcript levels.
147
,
148
One particular function of TDP‐43 is to bind to certain sites within pre‐mRNA to repress aberrant, cryptic splicing.
149
In most instances, cryptic splicing leads to an aberrant mRNA species which is subject to degradation.
Much of what was known about RNA dysregulation was based on various experimental models, in part because the number of neurons that exhibit TDP‐43 aggregates together with loss of normal nuclear TDP‐43 protein is relatively low at any given time, typically less than 5% of cellularity. Hypothesizing that identifying the changes associated with TDP‐43 pathology in affected human neurons from brain tissue would be important, a method was devised to isolate nuclei from frozen human brain tissue to isolate neuronal nuclei with pathologic nuclear clearance versus adjacent uninvolved neuronal nuclei by fluorescence activated nuclei sorting (Liu E et al., Cell Reports 2019). It was observed that 17.4% (5576 out of 31,898) of all RNA transcripts were differentially expressed in pathologic neuronal nuclei. Moreover, this dataset has been used to identify multiple important aberrant splicing and RNA processing defects. Most relevant to the development of biomarkers is the identification of cryptic splicing events which occur upon the loss of normal nuclear TDP‐43. While most of these cryptically spliced RNA species are degraded, some of these aberrant RNA species survive and are translated into protein. Detection of these aberrant protein species, most of which contain neoantigens which are not normally expressed, has been proposed as a biomarker of TDP‐43 dysfunction due to loss of normal nuclear TDP‐43 secondary to cytoplasmic TDP‐43 aggregation. Using human iPSC‐derived neurons after TDP‐43 knockdown together with our transcriptome dataset from sorted human brain tissue, others have now identified a set of cryptic splicing events that leads to the expression of proteins with neoantigens. Indeed, 18 de novo peptides derived from 13 genes could be detected in the CSF of ALS/FTD cases using mass spectrometry methods.
150
Similarly, an independent group has reported that cryptic HDGFL2 protein can be detected in the CSF and blood of ALS‐FTD cases using an immunoassay.
151
Additional studies are required to determine the sensitivity and specificity of these novel cryptic neoantigen detection assays as a biomarker of underlying TDP‐43 proteinopathy. While there is currently no robust biofluid marker of TDP 43 pathology, this should not be overly discouraging if we consider the effort and time it took to develop disease‐specific biofluid signatures for AD, and noting that such work is still ongoing today (e.g., the further characterization and evaluation of tau proteoforms in plasma). Fortunately, with established and carefully phenotyped cohorts, like the ADNI cohort, and with knowledge gained from parallel efforts for related neurodegenerative disorders, there is hope that we can “fast‐track” development for biomarkers for TDP‐43 pathology.
